children.text: The squeaking door

Squeaking is very common in everyday life: when closing doors, writing with chalk on a board, playing a violin, walking in new shoes, and in other situations. Here in Israel, the mechanisms responsible for squeaking also cause strong earthquakes that recur every few decades. These occur near the Dead Sea, just above the deepest known rift in Earth's crust.
The physical mechanism of squeaking lies in the difference between the coefficients of static and sliding friction. In this problem, we study this mechanism in the context of opening a door.
Part A. The simplest model
Consider the following system (see Fig. 1):
A body of mass $m$ is attached to a long ideal spring with spring constant $k$. The other end is pulled at constant speed $u$. The coefficient of static friction and
the coefficient of sliding friction against the surface are $\mu_s$
and $\mu_k$, respectively, with $\mu_k < \mu_s$.
The simplest model for studying squeaking
This simplest model admits two different regimes of motion:
1. Motion that always involves sliding. We call this regime pure sliding.

2. Motion that alternates between sliding and rest relative to the surface. We call this phenomenon stick-slip motion. Such stick-slip motion produces the squeaking sounds frequently encountered in everyday life.

Consider the case in which, initially at $t = 0$, the body is pulled along the floor at speed $v_0$, and the spring force balances the sliding friction force. Assume that $0 < v_0 < u$. The spring extension then varies periodically with time $t$.
A1
Find the period $T_0$ and amplitude $A$ of these oscillations.
A2
Sketch the spring extension as a function of time, $x(t)$, over the interval $0 < t < 3T_0$.
A3

Consider another case in which, initially at $t = 0$, the body is at rest and the initial spring extension $x$ is exactly the same as in parts A1-A2. Sketch the body's velocity relative to the surface as a function of time, $v(t)$, over the interval $0 < t < 3T$, where $T$ is the new period of oscillation of $x(t)$. Motion to the right corresponds to positive velocity $v$. Indicate the approximate position of the horizontal line $v = u$ on your graph.
A4
For the initial conditions of part A3, find the time-averaged spring extension $\overline{x}$ over one oscillation period.
A5
For the conditions of part A3, find the period $T$ of the oscillations of $x(t)$.
Stick-slip motion ceases at sufficiently large values of the speed $u$. Let us consider one possible mechanism for explaining this phenomenon.
A6

Assume that, during each oscillation period $T$, a small amount of the total oscillation energy is dissipated as heat. Let $\eta = | \Delta A / A|$ be the fractional loss of amplitude per period in the stick-slip regime. Assuming $\eta \ll 1$, find the critical speed $u_c$ at which \textbf{stick-slip motion} becomes impossible.
Do not include the damping considered in part A6 in the second part of this problem.
Part B. The squeaking door

A door hinge consists of a hollow, open-ended metal cylinder of radius $r$, height $h$, and wall thickness $\Delta r$. Its lower end rests on a metal support attached to the wall (the contact region is an annulus of radius $r$ and thickness $\Delta r \ll r$); see Fig. 2. The coefficients of sliding and static friction between the cylinder and its support are $\mu_k$ and $\mu_s$, respectively, with $\mu_k < \mu_s$. The upper end of the cylinder is rigidly attached to the door, which is treated as a perfectly rigid body. A door usually hangs on two or three hinges, but its weight is supported by only one hinge, which is the one that squeaks. The cylinder of this hinge presses on its metal support with a force equal to the weight of the entire door, whose mass is $M$.
Schematic diagram of the door
The deformed cylinder

The hinge cylinder itself is not perfectly rigid. It undergoes shear deformation without changing its overall shape, so that initially vertical line segments become inclined through a small angle $\alpha$ (see Fig. 3). The elastic force acting on an element of small area $dS$ due to this shear deformation is:
\begin{equation*}
dF = G \alpha dS,

\end{equation*} where $G$ is the shear modulus (a constant characterizing the material's elastic properties). For calculations, use $r = 5 \,мм$, $h = 3 \,см$, $\Delta r = 1 \, мм$, $\mu_s = 0.75$, $\mu_k = 0.55$, $G = 8 \cdot 10^{10} \,Па$, $M = 30 \,кг$, and $g = 9.8\, м/с^2$. Use the approximation $\Delta r \ll r$.
B1

The door starts turning very slowly from rest. For small angular displacements of the door, derive an expression for the torsional stiffness $\kappa = \tau / \theta$, where $\tau$ is the torque required to turn the door through an angle $\theta$.
B2

When the door rotates at a small angular velocity, it enters the stick-slip friction regime, emitting sound pulses: a squeak. Find the door's angular velocity $\Omega$ at which the sound frequency reaches the audible range, starting at $f = 20$ Hz. Assume that the frequency $f_0$ of the sound oscillations excited in the rod during sliding itself is high, so that $f_0 \gg f$. Obtain both analytical and numerical results.

children.text: A1
Find the period $T_0$ and amplitude $A$ of these oscillations.

The oscillations occur under a constant sliding friction force. They are therefore simple harmonic oscillations about a shifted equilibrium position. Their angular frequency is: \[\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}.\] Thus the oscillation period is:
Answer: \[T_0=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}=2\pi\sqrt\frac mk\]
The initial velocity of the body relative to the equilibrium position is: \[\left(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\right)_0=u-v_0.\] The oscillation amplitude is therefore:
Answer: \[A=\frac1{\omega_0}\left(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\right)_0=(u-v_0)\sqrt\frac mk\]
A2
Sketch the spring extension as a function of time, $x(t)$, over the interval $0 < t < 3T_0$.
The graph is sinusoidal, as shown below:
Answer:

The initial position is given by: \[x_0=\frac{\mu_kmg}{k},\] which is also the equilibrium position. Contestants are not required to find this value explicitly, but must understand that it is positive.
A3

Consider another case in which, initially at $t = 0$, the body is at rest and the initial spring extension $x$ is exactly the same as in parts A1-A2. Sketch the body's velocity relative to the surface as a function of time, $v(t)$, over the interval $0 < t < 3T$, where $T$ is the new period of oscillation of $x(t)$. Motion to the right corresponds to positive velocity $v$. Indicate the approximate position of the horizontal line $v = u$ on your graph.

The graph consists of slipping and sticking intervals. The slipping intervals are sinusoidal and join the horizontal sticking intervals with discontinuities in the first derivative at the junctions. The velocity maxima lie above the line $v=u$, because $u$ is the
average
velocity. Moreover, the maxima lie above $v=2u$, although contestants are not required to show this.
Answer:
A4
For the initial conditions of part A3, find the time-averaged spring extension $\overline{x}$ over one oscillation period.

In the reference frame of the far end of the spring, the body's position equals the negative of the spring extension $x$. The motion is an oscillation about the equilibrium position $x_0$. During slipping, the motion is sinusoidal; during sticking, the velocity is constant at $-u$. The regimes change at the point where the spring force balances the limiting static friction force, i.e.: \[x_s=\frac{\mu_smg}{k},\] and at the point symmetric to $x_s$ about $x_0$.
Thus the average spring extension equals the extension at equilibrium:
Answer: \[\bar x=x_0=\frac{\mu_kmg}{k}\]
A5
For the conditions of part A3, find the period $T$ of the oscillations of $x(t)$.

In the same reference frame, find the body's displacement during the sticking interval: \[2(x_s-x_0)=2(\mu_s-\mu_k)mg/k.\] Since the body's speed in this regime is $u$, the time spent sticking is: \[t_{stick}=\frac{2(\mu_s-\mu_k)mg}{ku}.\] During slipping, the motion is sinusoidal about $x_0$, with angular frequency $\omega_0$. The phase $\varphi$ at the transition to slipping is determined by the ratio of the body's position and velocity relative to $x_0$: \[\operatorname{tg}\varphi=\frac{\omega_0(x_s-x_0)}{u}=\frac{(\mu_s-\mu_k)g}{u}\sqrt\frac mk.\] Hence the time spent slipping is: \[t_{slip}=T_0\left(1-\frac\varphi\pi\right)=2\sqrt\frac mk\left(\pi-\operatorname{arctg}\left(\frac{(\mu_s-\mu_k)g}{u}\sqrt\frac mk\right)\right).\] The total oscillation period is:
Answer: \[T=t_{stick}+t_{slip}=2\sqrt\frac mk\left(\frac{(\mu_s-\mu_k)g}{u}\sqrt\frac mk\pi-\operatorname{arctg}\left(\frac{(\mu_s-\mu_k)g}{u}\sqrt\frac mk\right)\right)\]
A6

Assume that, during each oscillation period $T$, a small amount of the total oscillation energy is dissipated as heat. Let $\eta = | \Delta A / A|$ be the fractional loss of amplitude per period in the stick-slip regime. Assuming $\eta \ll 1$, find the critical speed $u_c$ at which \textbf{stick-slip motion} becomes impossible.

Continue in the same reference frame. While the body is slipping, the amplitude of its motion decreases slightly because of energy losses. At the start of the motion, the velocity is $-u$, and the phase is $\varphi$, found in the preceding part. Thus the initial velocity amplitude is $u/\cos\varphi$. For the body to enter the sticking regime, its velocity must return to $-u$, but the phase will then exceed $2\pi-\varphi$ because of the losses. In other words, losses lengthen the slipping interval. The limiting case occurs when the body reaches velocity $-u$ exactly at equilibrium (phase $2\pi$). Indeed, if the velocity at equilibrium is less than $-u$, the body continues along a damped sinusoid without ever returning to the sticking regime.

Since even small losses $\eta\ll1$ eliminate sticking, the fraction of time spent sticking must also be small. This corresponds to a large pulling speed $u$. Slipping then lasts for almost the entire oscillation period, during which the amplitude decreases by the fractional amount $\eta$ to a good approximation. At the limiting case, $u/\cos\varphi$ decreases to $u$, so: \[\eta=\left|\frac{\Delta A}A\right|=\left|\frac{u/\cos\varphi-u}{u/\cos\varphi}\right|=1-\cos\varphi\approx\varphi^2/2.\] Simplifying the expression for $\varphi$ in the small-angle approximation gives: \[\eta=\frac{m(\mu_s-\mu_k)^2g^2}{2ku_c^2}\implies\]
Answer: \[u_c=(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{\frac{m}{2k\eta}}\]

Alternatively, derive $u_c$ by explicitly writing the initial amplitude $A$ of the harmonic oscillations: \[u_c=\omega_0A(1-\eta),\quad A^2=(x_s-x_0)^2+\frac mk u_c^2.\] Finally, the fractional energy loss $|\Delta E/E|=2\eta$ may simply be written as: \[2\eta\cdot \frac12mu_c^2=\frac12 k(x_s-x_0)^2.\]
B1

The door starts turning very slowly from rest. For small angular displacements of the door, derive an expression for the torsional stiffness $\kappa = \tau / \theta$, where $\tau$ is the torque required to turn the door through an angle $\theta$.

For small angular displacements of the door, the lower end of the cylinder remains stationary. When the cylinder is sheared through an angle $\alpha$, its upper end moves tangentially by $h\alpha$. This corresponds to a door rotation $\theta=h\alpha/r$. The elastic shear force acting on an area element $\mathrm dA$ of the cylinder's lower end is: \[\mathrm dF=G\alpha\,\mathrm dA=\frac{Gr}{h}\theta\,\mathrm dA.\] This produces a torque: \[\mathrm d\tau=r\,\mathrm dF=\frac{Gr^2}{h}\theta\,\mathrm dA.\] The total torque is: \[\tau=\frac{Gr^2}{h}\theta\cdot2\pi r\Delta r=\frac{2\pi Gr^3\Delta r}{h}\theta.\] Thus the torsional stiffness is:
Answer: \[\kappa=\frac{2\pi Gr^3\Delta r}{h}\approx2000~Н\cdot м\]
Contestants are not required to calculate the numerical value. Any expression giving the correct result in the limit $\Delta r\ll r$ is accepted.
B2

When the door rotates at a small angular velocity, it enters the stick-slip friction regime, emitting sound pulses: a squeak. Find the door's angular velocity $\Omega$ at which the sound frequency reaches the audible range, starting at $f = 20$ Hz. Assume that the frequency $f_0$ of the sound oscillations excited in the rod during sliding itself is high, so that $f_0 \gg f$. Obtain both analytical and numerical results.
Neglecting the duration of the sticking interval, we obtain, by analogy with the derivation in part
A
:\[t_{stick}=\frac{2(\mu_s-\mu_k)Mgr}{\kappa\Omega}\implies\]
Answer: \[\Omega=\frac{2(\mu_s-\mu_k)Mgr}{\kappa t_{stick}}=\frac{2(\mu_s-\mu_k)Mgrf}{\kappa}=\frac{(\mu_s-\mu_k)Mghf}{\pi Gr^2\Delta r}=5.6\cdot10^{-3}~с^{-1}.\]

Any expression giving the correct result in the limit $\Delta r\ll r$ is accepted. Numerical answers may differ because $\Delta r/r=0.2$ cannot be considered very small. Numerical answers must therefore be checked by substituting the values given in the problem into the contestant's expression.
